units.citation: World Bank (2009). Bulgaria - Wetlands Restoration and Pollution Reduction Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report. Report No. ICR1004. World Bank, Washington DC. 23 June 2009.
units.quote:
Two months after the 
flooding the PNP reported an increase of key indicator species, and an increased diversity and 
quantity of bird and fish species. According to PNP reports, after the flooding by June 2008, 10 
new fish species entered the restored area. Nesting pairs of the ferruginous duck increased from 5 
to 50, and mallard ducks from 16 to 400. Some rare bird species have returned, including the 
purple heron and glossy ibis.

context.practice_as_described: restoration of 4,035 ha of former Danube floodplain marshes (Belene Island, Persina Nature Park; Kalimok-Brushlen) by building infrastructure to regulate water flows and allow controlled flooding of former marshes, with protected-area management plans and Natura 2000 designation
context.note: Persina Nature Park reports cited in the self-evaluation ICR; before-after only, two months after first flooding (April 2008). Income group high (Bulgaria) - transfer handled by the envelope. IEG review (wb_ieg_icrr_bulgaria_wetlands_restoration_2011) calls the biodiversity outcomes anecdotal rather than factual.

units.quote:

water marsh, restored peatlands and rewetted peatlands had

context.note: assumes steady CO2 and CH4 fluxes over time (authors' stated limitation); switchover approach after Neubauer & Megonigal; studies with positive NEE excluded from the model (Figure 6 caption), so the range is conditional on the site being a CO2 sink at all

units.citation: Tan et al. (2020). Conversion of coastal wetlands, riparian wetlands, and peatlands increases greenhouse gas emissions: A global meta‐analysis. Global Change Biology.
units.quote:
However, the LULCC types of CW, CL, and AP increased 
the GWPs by 7.8, 22.3, and 29.5 times on average that in NCWs, re-
spectively, turning to a strong greenhouse effect.

relationship.outcome_raw: comprehensive global warming potential (carbon dioxide + methane + nitrous oxide, carbon-dioxide-equivalent) of natural coastal wetlands after conversion to constructed wetlands, cropland or aquaculture ponds: GWP multiplied, i.e. net climate benefit lost

context.practice_as_described: no intervention studied: existing natural wetlands compared with the same wetland types converted to cropland, pasture, aquaculture ponds, constructed wetlands or drained
context.note: Global meta-analysis of 209 sites: GHG fluxes of natural coastal wetlands (NCW), riparian wetlands (NRW) and peatlands (NPL) vs the same wetland types converted to constructed wetlands (CW), cropland (CL), aquaculture ponds (AP), drained wetlands (DW) and pasture (PAS). A LOSS study of EXISTING wetlands: no restoration was measured; the engine flips loss-framed signs. GWP100 per IPCC 2013. Pooled across countries - no country/income tag. Natural coastal wetlands averaged -0.9 t CO2-eq/ha/yr (a net sink). Mechanism: enclosure and drainage cut tidal flooding and salinity; ecosystem respiration rises more than GPP.

units.quote:
After the construction of the SEMRY scheme, just over 7,000 fishing households remained in the
floodplain, catching an average of 15 sacks of wet fish a year from flood-dependent wetland areas.
This increased to 10,400 households catching 29 sacks after pilot flood release

relationship.outcome_raw: annual catch of wet fish per fishing household from flood-dependent wetland areas, before vs after the pilot flood releases

context.practice_as_described: Floodplain re-inundation (hydrological restoration): two pilot flood releases by the IUCN Waza Logone project re-opening river channels cut off by the embankment of the SEMRY rice scheme below the Maga dam - the Petit Guruma in 1994 (about 20 m3/s) and the Areitekele in 1997 (about 10 m3/s) - re-flooding about 180-200 km2 of floodplain in an average year. Baseline = the reduced-flood regime after the dam (1979-1993).
context.note: IUCN project book written by the implementing project's own staff and consultants (grey literature; positive-bias risk, self-assessed results). Household surveys before/after the pilot releases (IUCN 2002 valuation study, chapter 11 by L. Emerton); fishing households also rose from about 7,000 to 10,400. Same section: households consume just under 6 sacks of wet fish a year each (p136) - a food-supply link. p119: 'fishers caught 1,777 tonnes of fish in the additional 200 km2 of flooded area', 1.5 to 2 times typical inland floodplain yields (same survey, not emitted separately). Sack weight not stated. Confound: wetter years 1994-1997. Mechanism: larger, longer floods extend spawning and feeding habitat and the fishing season. Projection to 32 sacks with full re-flooding is not emitted (ex-ante).

units.quote:
Many wetlands exist because they overlie impermeable 
soils or rocks and there is little interaction with 
groundwater. The database contains 69 statements

context.note: Vote count of functional statements from the review's database (Table 5, pp7-8, 'number of functional statements for each wetland type'); the table's OCR is not in row/column order, so the counts are taken from the Conclusions text. A count of studies is not an effect size: strength unspecified. The authors warn (p5) that counts are not inter-compared, that some functions are studied more than others, and that the sample is dominated by North America. Comparator existing_wetland: home family per comparator_policy, out of the roll-up. Only the comparison with other land types is an effect (more 6 / less 9). The 32 'recharge takes place' and 18 'no recharge' statements describe presence of a process with no counterfactual (catalogue #28) and are not encoded. Mechanism in the quote: many wetlands overlie impermeable soils or rocks with little groundwater interaction; floodplains on sandy soils (India, West Africa) recharge when flooded.

units.citation: Loth, P. (Ed.) (2004). The Return of the Water: Restoring the Waza Logone Floodplain in Cameroon. IUCN, Gland and Cambridge. xvi + 156 pp.
units.quote:
Surveys that were held among different ethnic groups from 1996 to 1998 showed that the breeding rate
of animals grazing in the floodplain had improved over this period. For cows, it increased from 16 %
in 1996 to 50 % in 1998. It remained stable at this level up to date (2000). For the small ruminants, the
breeding rate was 15% in 1994, increased to 32% in 1996 and reached 50% in 1998. The increase of
the reproductive rates of livestock coincided with the improved conditions of the floodplain grasslands,
which resulted from the pilot flood releases undertaken by the Waza Logone project in 1994 and 1997.

relationship.outcome_raw: annual breeding (reproductive) rate of cows grazing the floodplain, 1996 vs 1998, after the pilot flood releases improved the grasslands

context.practice_as_described: Floodplain re-inundation (hydrological restoration): two pilot flood releases by the IUCN Waza Logone project re-opening river channels cut off by the embankment of the SEMRY rice scheme below the Maga dam - the Petit Guruma in 1994 (about 20 m3/s) and the Areitekele in 1997 (about 10 m3/s) - re-flooding about 180-200 km2 of floodplain in an average year. Baseline = the reduced-flood regime after the dam (1979-1993).
context.note: IUCN project book written by the implementing project's own staff and consultants (grey literature; positive-bias risk, self-assessed results). Repeated surveys before/after with no control area; the authors say the rise 'coincided with' the pilot releases. Small ruminants 15% (1994) to 32% (1996) to 50% (1998), same quote. Confounds named in the book: 1994-1997 were wetter than any year since the dam, and the model later showed the wetter years were 'as much a reason for the extra flooding as the pilot release itself' (p117). Mechanism: re-flooding restored perennial grasses (cover 41% to 61%, p119, citing Scholte et al. 2000b) and dry-season pasture, so animals were in better condition. Cattle numbers in the floodplain rose 260% since 1994 (p119), but partly from an influx of herds from Nigeria (+130% herds) - not emitted. Strength capped by unreplicated before/after design.

units.citation: Bullock et al. (2003). The role of wetlands in the hydrological cycle. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences.
units.quote:
There is strong evidence that wetlands evaporate more 
water that other land types, such as forests, savannah 
grassland or arable land. Two thirds of studies (48 of 
74) conclude that wetlands increase average annual 
evaporation or reduce average annual river flow. About 
10% of studies (7) conclude the opposite; for example 
some woodlands in Zambia had greater evaporation than 
the adjacent wetlands. The remaining 25% are neutral. 
There is no obvious distinction amongst different 
wetland sub-types or geographical regions of the world.

relationship.outcome_raw: the opposite (less evaporation / more annual flow than the adjacent land) in about 10% of studies (7), e.g. Zambian woodlands evaporating more than adjacent wetlands

context.practice_as_described: EXISTING freshwater wetlands of all hydrological types (floodplain and headwater; lakes excluded, p2). No intervention: studies of what existing wetlands do. BASELINE: other land types or non-wetland parts of the catchment (forest, savannah grassland, arable land), or the catchment without the wetland.
context.note: Vote count of functional statements from the review's database (Table 5, pp7-8, 'number of functional statements for each wetland type'); the table's OCR is not in row/column order, so the counts are taken from the Conclusions text. A count of studies is not an effect size: strength unspecified. The authors warn (p5) that counts are not inter-compared, that some functions are studied more than others, and that the sample is dominated by North America. Comparator existing_wetland: home family per comparator_policy, out of the roll-up. Mechanism in the quote: wetlands evaporate more water than forest, savannah grassland or arable land, so less water leaves as river flow. Annual water balance; no hazard_type. water_yield direction is 'context' (more flow is good or bad by setting). Reversal kept.

relationship.outcome_raw: summer low flows (weekly-average minima) at sub-watershed outlets under future climate: restoration raises the low flows that climate change lowers (Jaune sub-watershed illustrated)

context.practice_as_described: Wetland restoration scenarios: 'adding coverage in the landscape' - wetland area increased by 20, 50, 100 and 150% proportionally to the initial isolated/riparian ratio and placed at current wetland locations, replacing forest, agricultural or open land (not impervious surfaces) (p5-6, p10). BASELINE: same future climate (47 projections, 2020-2059 and 2060-2099) without restoration (R0), and the 1980-2019 reference period.
context.note: Modelled (PHYSITEL/HYDROTEL semi-distributed model, calibrated per sub-watershed, 47 climate projections, 1979-2099). Watershed: forest 54%, urban 28%, agriculture 3%, wetlands 6% (p2-3), so farming_system is left blank and the result is a catchment-outlet flow effect, not an on-farm one. Effects are reported as compensation trajectories (Fig. 4) and restoration targets (20 to 150% more wetland), not as a flow-change magnitude in the text, so no magnitude is encoded. Low flows are named 'summer drought events' by the authors (p6: 'In the case of summer drought events, all sub-watersheds show more severe low flows in the future'). Recorded as water_yield (streamflow measured), not drought_hazard, so XW routes it to catchment_water_yield and to T3 drought as a proxy. p8: 'wetland restoration helps to mitigate ... reductions of low flows in all sub-watersheds', but full compensation needs 50 to >150% more wetland and is generally not reached for 2060-2099 (p8). Less severe low flows (Q2-7) are compensated more easily than severe ones (Q10-7) (p9, p11). Counter-finding emitted separately (_3).

units.quote:
In 2019, the hotspot density in peatlands restored with dams (5 km−2) was significantly lower than in
matched unrestored areas (6 km−2, p < 0.05).

relationship.outcome_raw: El Nino fire hotspot density after restoration (first post-restoration El Nino), peat restored with canal dams vs matched unrestored drained peat

context.practice_as_described: Rewetting by canal blocking: canal dams (drainage blocking) installed by BRGM and partners 2016-2023 (8,014 dams). BASELINE: matched drained peatland without restoration, same 100-km grid, similar 2015 hotspot density and land cover (p2-4).
context.note: Quasi-experimental: 0.5 x 0.5 km cells within 250 m of restoration infrastructure matched to drained, unrestored cells in the same 100-km grid with similar 2015 hotspot density (+-10%) and land cover, then difference-in-differences (p2-4). Outcome = VIIRS active-fire hotspot density (km-2) in El Nino years (2015 pre, 2019 and 2023 post). Restoration was targeted at densely drained, high-fire peat (p5). SRC.study_country is blank for this source; IDN is stated on p2. DiD restoration effect for dams in 2019: -1.1 km-2 (p < 0.05) (p5). Subgroups of the same data (not separate units, #61): significant only where >=4 dams (-1.7 km-2), 1-year-old dams -2.2 km-2 (p = 0.002), 2-year-old dams not significant, insignificant in most land covers except NVO (-5.3 km-2), stronger in the south (p5); effect only within the 0.25 km2 cells around dams, none in larger cells (p5). Dams plus wells reduced 2019 hotspots by 22% across 3,920 km2 and account for 38% of the 2015-2019 reduction (p7, p9) - combined figure kept here, not emitted. Cropland: restored areas still showed a (smaller) reduction while unrestored cropland rose (p8). Authors suggest dams are less effective in strong El Nino years (p8, speculative - not encoded).

relationship.outcome_raw: household TRANSFER income (pensions, agricultural subsidies, ecological compensation) of farmers participating in wetland restoration, propensity-score matched (kernel matching)

context.practice_as_described: 'returning farmland to lakes': farmers withdraw from residential areas and cultivated land formed by reclaiming land from lakes, which are restored to natural lakes on a large scale to improve the wetland ecosystem; most surveyed farmers received no continuous subsidy
context.note: balanced panel of 365 households surveyed in 2018 and 2021 around the Poyang Lake wetland; two-way fixed-effect model plus propensity-score matching (k-nearest-neighbour, kernel/'nuclear' and radius) to correct self-selection. The outcome is the natural logarithm of household income in Yuan (plus 1), so an ATT is a log difference and is read here as a log response ratio. All three matching methods agree in sign and are within a few hundredths of each other; the kernel row is used throughout for consistency. Table 2 of the same paper gives the two-way fixed-effect coefficient on total income as -0.257 (p<0.1) without controls and -0.171 (not significant) with them. WHO GAINS: transfer income is the only component that rises, significantly, under every matching method. Transfer income is defined on page 7 as pensions, agricultural subsidies, ecological compensation and compensation for migrant-bird damage — so the gain is the compensation channel, not production. The paper notes most surveyed farmers received no continuous restoration subsidy and that fishing-ban compensation covered only one year.

units.quote:
Sedge communities on the peatland Dokudovskoe (1,200 ha) occupy no more 
than 20 ha 
End of Project Target  
Sedge communities on peatland Dokudovskoe occupy at least 700 ha 
End of Project Status 
By 2020, pilot activities on creation of sedge communities underway on 950 
hectares of cultivated peat bog. Dokudovskoe  peatland rewetted (950 ha). 
Activities for accelerated restoration of open sedge marshes were planned 
for an area of about 700 ha in 2021, using machinery for soil preparation, 
collection and sowing of seeds of marsh plants. However, for three years in 
the natural bogs of Sporoske and Zvanets sedge seeds were practically absent 
for unknown reasons. Therefore, marsh plants were planted and a small 
amount of sedge seeds were used on an area of 70 ha.  
On the rest of the area prepared for planting of marsh plants seeds, 
restoration took place naturally. In this regard, reed and cattail were the first 
to appear on these areas, which in the process of development will be 
replaced by sedge communities  
Mapping of vegetation in the Dokudovskoe  peatland conducted in July-
August 2021; 2021-2022 monitoring activities determined the area of 
reinstated bog plant communities: Phragmites-sedge communities (Carex 
acuta, C. rostrata, C. pseudocyperus, Phragmites australis) on peatland 
Dokudovskoe occupy at least 398 ha (botanical report).

context.note: Target (700 ha) about 60% achieved: sedge seed was practically absent in donor bogs for three years, so most of the area was left to natural succession, with reed and cattail colonising first. The vegetation is a habitat-structure outcome, not a species count.

units.citation: Pang et al. (2022). Policy Cognition, Household Income and Farmers’ Satisfaction: Evidence from a Wetland Ecological Compensation Project in the Poyang Lake Area at the Micro Level. Sustainability.
units.quote:
Of the surveyed rural households, 56.9% thought that household incomes decreased
after participating in the policy, 38.3% thought that household incomes did not change
and only 4.8% thought that household incomes increased. The results indicate that most
rural households believed that household incomes decreased after participating in the
wetland ecological compensation policy. The policy has no positive impacts on household
incomes, which is attributed to the low compensation rates for most farmers.

relationship.outcome_raw: share of surveyed households reporting that household income DECREASED after joining the wetland ecological compensation policy (most of the rest reported no change, very few an increase); the authors attribute the loss to low compensation rates

context.practice_as_described: wetland ecological compensation policies at Poyang Lake: a 2014 pilot that compensates for the ecological benefits of wetlands, alongside the national programme returning farmland to wetlands, a lake-wide fishing moratorium and migratory-bird habitat protection; compensation is paid mainly in cash to arable landowners and the community
context.note: Cross-sectional household survey, 773 households, 27 villages, July 2019; ordered-logit on policy satisfaction. Income change is the household's OWN PERCEPTION of change since joining the policy - no counterfactual, no measured income. PICOS: the paper does not separate restoration (farmland returned to wetland) from conservation compensation for existing wetland (bird-habitat protection, fishing ban), so attribution = bundled. THE TRANSFER PATTERN: the household outcome is governed by the compensation rate, not by production - here the transfer is too low to make most households whole (65.7% rate the compensation low or very low, operational unit ev_wgy_poy_op1). Corroborates Feng et al. 2024 (same lake), where transfer income was the only component that rose. Perception shares set no strength class.

units.quote:

relationship.outcome_raw: protective effect of coastal wetlands against a TROPICAL STORM (the weak end of the cyclone scale): elasticity of property damage with respect to wetland area

context.note: decomposition of the wetland elasticity by storm intensity; the paper reports -0.58 tropical storm, -0.55 cat 1, -0.40 cat 2, -0.35 cat 3-5, i.e. protection is proportionately LARGER for weaker storms; the parenthetical gloss in the source sentence ('a 1% decrease in wetlands is associated with a 0.58% reduction in property damages') contradicts the sign of the elasticity it glosses and is read here as a typographical slip in the source - the claim encoded is the stated elasticity

units.citation: Evans et al. (2021). Overriding water table control on managed peatland greenhouse gas emissions. Nature.
units.quote:
We also evaluated an ‘optimal re-wetting’ scenario, in which all areas currently under cropland and 
grassland are re-wetted to a mean WTDe of 10 cm to maximise their net climate change mitigation 
potential (Figure 1d). This scenario would generate net CO2 uptake of 106 Mt CO2 yr-1, but with an 
offsetting emission of 91 Mt CO2 yr-1 of CH4 emissions, giving a small net GHG removal.

relationship.outcome_raw: optimal re-wetting of all peat cropland and grassland: a net CARBON DIOXIDE uptake of 106 Mt carbon dioxide yr-1 against an offsetting METHANE emission of 91 Mt carbon dioxide yr-1, leaving only a small net greenhouse-gas removal — BOTH GASES quantified, and the methane term eats most of the carbon gain

context.practice_as_described: raising the water table in managed peatland — the paper spans 'a broad gradient of land-use intensity from near-natural bogs and fens to intensive grassland, cropland and peat extraction' (including conservation-managed and re-wetted sites) and evaluates two management scenarios: an 'agricultural mitigation' scenario halving drainage depths while keeping the land in production, and an 'optimal re-wetting' scenario taking cropland and grassland on peat to a mean effective water-table depth of 10 cm
context.note: 16 UK eddy-covariance peatland flux towers plus 49 published temperate/boreal EC studies (n = 65) for CO2 and 41 annual CH4 flux measurements from the UK and Ireland; empirical WTDe relationships then applied to global drained cropland and grassland areas; global scenario over 29.0 Mha of drained peat cropland and grassland; CH4 converted at GWP100 = 28 per Table 1; climate_zone blank because the scenario spans boreal, temperate and tropical, and income_group blank because the tropical component is extrapolated rather than measured | gas/baseline tag 2026-10-16: net CO2 uptake of 106 Mt CO2 yr-1, but with an offsetting emission of 91 Mt CO2 yr-1 of CH4 emissions, giving a small net GHG removal

relationship.outcome_raw: ceiling on the carbon-loss reduction obtainable by raising water tables inside a drained peat plantation, relative to current emissions

context.practice_as_described: "improved plantation water management" — raising the average plantation water table to 0.6 m depth, described as near the highest water levels achievable inside a drained Acacia / oil palm plantation. units.quote:
Because of the high rate of root respiration, raising the (ground)water level hardly results in 
12 
any emission reduction in peat surface CO2 fluxes.

relationship.outcome_raw: peat surface carbon dioxide flux in a drained forest when the groundwater level is raised — hardly any emission reduction, because root respiration dominates the flux

context.practice_as_described: "Dams are of the so-called cofferdam type, consisting of a frame made of galam poles filled with compacted peat" — six dams built by manual labour (four in the East-west Canal, two in the Kalampangan Canal) from indigenous materials, galam timber (Melaleuca cajuputi) and peat (gambut), designed as weirs rather than water-storing dams; "The side slopes, tops and banks were planted with Red Balau (Shorea balangeran)".
context.note: a NULL kept deliberately, and a direct qualifier on the rewetting-cuts-emissions story: in a DRAINED FOREST the surface CO2 flux is dominated by root respiration, so raising the water level barely moves it. context.note: Before-after figure for one site with no comparison area (unreplicated). Bundled: fire patrols and the State Forestry Department's own fire control are in the same bundle as drain blocking, and the report gives no share for drain blocking (component_share_pct not stated -> flat bundle weight). Patrols that stop land clearing and ignition may explain much of the drop; a reviewer may judge drain blocking a minor component and exclude. The 98% figure (2014-2022) is uncited; the paragraph cites Nath et al. 2017 and Alam et al. 2021 for the CBO, which predate 2022, so the figure's primary is unknown - possibly programme self-reporting (positive-bias risk). No fire-season severity stated; 2015 and 2019 were El Nino fire years in the region but the report does not say so (not inferred). Effect locus: off-site/landscape (forest fire extent), protected-area context - the rewetting is in a peat swamp forest, not on farmland.

units.quote:

context.note: Weighted meta-analysis of 28 studies / 59 effect sizes (Fisher z of r; not banded here), 17 empirical and 11 modelling studies, mostly North America and Europe; pooled across countries - no country/income tag. units.quote:
(i) quantify the impacts of wetlands on extreme flood and severe drought and (2) 
investigate the influences of geographical location and types of wetlands on their regulation ef­
ficiency. The hydrological modeling was conducted with various wetland loss scenarios on the 
Nenjiang River Basin (NRB)- a large river basin where wetlands are abundant and play an 
important hydrological regulation function. Modeling results showed that RWs mainly decreased 
peak flow and reduced downstream flood volume. However, IWs predominantly decreased flood 
volume and slightly mitigated peak flow in the entire NRB. For severe drought, RWs overall 
alleviated drought while IWs could intensify drought deficit to some extent.

units.citation: Stachowicz et al. (2022). To store or to drain — To lose or to gain? Rewetting drained peatlands as a measure for increasing water storage in the transboundary Neman River Basin. Science of The Total Environment.
units.quote:
Applying multiple assumptions, it was revealed that
rewetting drained peatlands in the Neman River Basin could increase water retention by 23.6–118 M m3. This corre-
sponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea. Unit increase of water retention
volume due to rewetting ranged between 69 and 344 m3·ha−1.

relationship.outcome_raw: additional water retained in the landscape after rewetting drained peatland (water-table rise around blocked ditches times peat porosity), per hectare; basin total equals a small fraction of annual river discharge

context.practice_as_described: rewetting of drained peatlands (fens and bogs) by blocking drainage ditches: simple ditch blocks of wood and peat (non-regulated outflow) or sophisticated blocks with water-level regulation, at stacking (damming) heights of 0.1, 0.3 or 0.5 m, across the Neman basin
context.note: Basin-scale GIS model over 8885 drained-peatland polygons, 18 scenarios (radius of water-level rise from the ditch, peat porosity, stacking height); water storage valued at reservoir replacement cost (EUR/m3/yr). Income: LTU/POL/RUS high, BLR upper-middle (most of the cost falls in Belarus). Range = mean retained volume at stacking heights 0.1 to 0.5 m (Table 1). Mechanism: blocked ditches raise the water level in the peat, which stores water in its pore space.

units.quote:
There is strong evidence that wetlands evaporate more 
water that other land types, such as forests, savannah 
grassland or arable land. Two thirds of studies (48 of 
74) conclude that wetlands increase average annual 
evaporation or reduce average annual river flow. About 
10% of studies (7) conclude the opposite; for example 
some woodlands in Zambia had greater evaporation than 
the adjacent wetlands. The remaining 25% are neutral. 
There is no obvious distinction amongst different

relationship.outcome_raw: per capita annual household income of farmers who gave up cultivated land to wetland restoration, propensity-score matched against non-participants (kernel matching)

context.practice_as_described: 'returning farmland to lakes': farmers withdraw from residential areas and cultivated land formed by reclaiming land from lakes, which are restored to natural lakes on a large scale to improve the wetland ecosystem; most surveyed farmers received no continuous subsidy
context.note: balanced panel of 365 households surveyed in 2018 and 2021 around the Poyang Lake wetland; two-way fixed-effect model plus propensity-score matching (k-nearest-neighbour, kernel/'nuclear' and radius) to correct self-selection. The outcome is the natural logarithm of household income in Yuan (plus 1), so an ATT is a log difference and is read here as a log response ratio. All three matching methods agree in sign and are within a few hundredths of each other; the kernel row is used throughout for consistency. Table 2 of the same paper gives the two-way fixed-effect coefficient on total income as -0.257 (p<0.1) without controls and -0.171 (not significant) with them. The strongest measured household signal in this lane: per capita income is lower for participants at the 1% level under all three matching methods, while total household income is not — the household absorbed the loss by putting more members to work.

context.practice_as_described: natural flood management measures grouped by purpose; the wetland-relevant groups are peatland restoration including gully blocking and floodplain restoration/reconnection, offline storage areas (water retention/detention ponds) and online storage areas (grip blocking, drainage/ditch blocking, buffer strips, beaver dams)
context.note: this CONTRADICTS Dadson et al. 2017 head-on and the review says so. It is the counter-argument to 'catchment-scale benefit at large events is unproven' — but it is a null correlation over a heterogeneous all-NFM corpus dominated by modelling, not a demonstration of benefit, and the review itself says large-scale research is still lacking. Direction recorded as negative because the pooled corpus reports reduction; the no-decay finding is the moderation result, carried here in the note
